entities.name: Henry Baldwin
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry Baldwin (1780–1844) was an American lawyer, Congressman, and jurist who served as Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court (1830–1844) — appointed by President Andrew Jackson. A Pennsylvania Federalist-turned-Jacksonian, Baldwin brought a complex and sometimes erratic jurisprudence to the Court — he was personally close to Jackson but often disagreed with the Democratic Party's constitutional positions, producing opinions that defied easy categorization.

Baldwin had been a prominent Pittsburgh lawyer and Congressman (1817–1822) before his Court appointment. His industrial Pittsburgh perspective — representing a manufacturing district with interests in protective tariffs and internal improvements — sometimes put him at odds with the Southern Jacksonian mainstream.

His mental health was unstable — he suffered breakdowns that intermittently prevented him from sitting — and he died in poverty despite his high office, an unusual fate for a Supreme Court Justice.

He wrote a significant constitutional law treatise ('A General View of the Origin and Nature of the Constitution') in 1837.
